title: Core D: Biomarker and Bio-Informatics Core
text:
Core D - Project Narrative
Myeloproliferative Neoplasms, which include myelofibrosis, are clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders with
limited therapeutic options currently; there is thus a need to develop innovate therapeutic approaches requiring
efforts using rational, targeted therapies in order to maximize therapeutic efficacy. The MPN-RC seeks to
develop novel therapeutic strategies and understand the disease biology of myelofibrosis. Core D will carry out
dynamic analyses of mechanism-based biomarkers, including genomic studies, which pertain to each of the
biologic and clinical studies proposed by the MPN-RC, allowing these studies to assess the mechanistic impact
of specific therapeutic interventions.

title: Signaling control and cellular basis of craniofacial morphogenesis and congenital disease
text:
Craniofacial congenital anomalies are amongst the most common birth defects, but current treatments remain
limited to surgical correction; this is in part due to a lack of understanding of the way cells move to give rise to
craniofacial structures and how these behaviors are controlled. We have established new approaches that allow
us to observe cell behaviors during craniofacial morphogenesis in mouse embryos. These techniques give us
an unprecedented view of craniofacial morphogenesis, which ultimately may lead us to discover new approaches
to treating these common conditions.

title: Quantitative Science Shared Resource
text: QUANTITATIVE SCIENCE SHARED RESOURCE (QSSR) The Quantitative Sciences Shared Resource (QSSR) was created in 2006 at the inception of the Dan L Duncan Comprehensive Cancer Center (DLDCCC) with the primary purpose of supporting its mission “to reduce the burden of cancer through exceptional patient care, outstanding education, innovative research, and community outreach and education”. Although our efforts directly or indirectly support all DLDCCC Strategic Pillars, we are especially focused on supporting the research mission of the Cancer Center. Our five specific aims address biostatistics, bioinformatics, high-performance computing, integration with other SRs, and support of scientific review, education, and training. Aim 1: Provide state-of-the-art biostatistical design, analysis, and interpretation to clinical, translational, and basic science cancer-related research; Aim 2: Provide state-of-the-art bioinformatic design, analysis, and interpretation to clinical, translational, and basic science cancer-related research; Aim 3: Provide access to high-quality, professionally managed, high-performance computing; Aim 4: Coordinate with other SRs to meet their analytic and data management needs; and Aim 5: Assist the DLDCCC with education, training, scientific review, data monitoring, and strategic planning. The QSSR is a critical resource to the Cancer Center, as we continue to contribute to virtually every aspect of its endeavors, from basic through clinical research and the coordination of data flows with other SRs. Areas of special emphasis and accomplishments include modernization of clinical trial design, expansion of support for single-cell-omic and spatial transcriptomic analysis, enhanced and upgraded high-performance computing capabilities, routine processing of raw data generated by other SRs, and major contributions to user training and education. We are well represented among DLDCCC leadership, as Dr. Hilsenbeck is a long-standing member of the Breast Cancer Program and serves on the DLDCCC Executive Committee; Dr. Coarfa is Co-Lead for Theme 2 in the Chromatin Biology Program and is a designated Program “Emerging Leader”; Dr. Wang is a member of the Cancer Cell and Gene Therapy (CCGT) Program and statistician of record for CCGT investigator-initiated trials; and Dr. Creighton is a member of the Tumor Biology Program and their primary contact for cancer bioinformatics. QSSR members also serve on various DLDCCC committees and review groups, which positions us to effectively advise the DLDCCC on strategic initiatives and to respond to new or changing priorities. In the most recent fiscal year, QSSR personnel assisted 169 DLDCCC investigators and were supported by more than 120 different peer-reviewed grants and other sources of chargeback. Since the last competing renewal, QSSR members authored or co-authored 160 peer-reviewed, cancer-related publications, with >50 in the highest-impact (IF>10) cancer journals. The breadth of QSSR activities and numbers of funded collaborations, unique users, and co-authored publications clearly demonstrate our value added to the DLDCCC.

title: Metabolic syndrome, chronic inflammation, and gout: a multi-omics approach
text:
Gout is an increasingly common, costly, and painful inflammatory condition which frequently co-
exists with the metabolic (insulin resistance) syndrome and its cardiometabolic sequalae, but
fundamental questions remain about what drives its development and the progression from
asymptomatic hyperuricemia to clinical gout. This Pathway to Independence Award will focus on
applying a multi-omics approach, integrating genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics, and
proteomics, to comprehensively investigate the relationships between metabolic syndrome,
chronic inflammation, and gout. This rigorous, cutting-edge approach, leveraging large genome-
wide association studies, prospective cohorts with decades of follow-up, and rich dietary and
biorepository data, will provide novel insights into gout disease mechanisms (e.g., genetic
variants and metabolic and inflammatory pathways), thereby laying a foundation for new
strategies to treat and prevent gout and its cardiometabolic comorbidities.

title: Translational Platform for Epilepsy Therapy and Biomarker Discovery
text:
There is currently no therapy that can prevent the development of epilepsy after brain trauma. Here we propose
to test the efficacy of a novel compound, and determine its efficacy and tolerability in an animal model of
posttraumatic epilepsy, in a setting that resembles the clinical practice of care of people with severe traumatic
brain injury. We also aim to identify and validate novel biomarkers that can predict who will develop epilepsy and
who may respond to a treatment that can prevent epilepsy, in hope that this may accelerate and optimize future
efforts to develop new antiepileptogenic therapies.

title: A multidisciplinary BCC for ovarian cancer early detection: translating discoveries to clinical use with a by-design approach
text:
This application aims to establish a biomarker characterization center to identify biomarkers in clinically easily
accessible samples and to develop them into clinical tests to capture high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (the
most common and deadliest form of ovarian cancer) at the early stages when surgical and therapeutic
treatment may still be able to change a patient’s long-term survival. The initial development and testing will be
in high-risk women population.

title: Mimicking, Exploiting, and Understanding Biology's Dynamic Heterogeneity in 4D
text:
Biological processes are regulated through intricate signaling events that vary in time and 3D space (i.e., 4D).
This project pioneers generalizable efforts to mimic, exploit, and quantify biology’s 4D complexity, paving the
way to new therapeutic targets and treatments of disease through a fundamentally transformed knowledge of
basic cell physiology. Critically, the methods being developed and implemented are cell-, tissue-, and disease-
agnostic, enabling enhanced understanding of a wide variety of biological processes while laying the
foundation for advances in disease diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.

title: Engineering human-derived programmable RNA effectors to retune gene expression
text:
RNA-targeting gene therapies that precise tune gene expression at the transcript level can address the
shortfalls and challenges of current gene therapies, but the large size and microbially-derived nature of existing
programmable RNA-targeting systems preclude broad clinical utility. Constructed from human protein parts,
CIRTS (CRISPR/Cas-inspired RNA targeting system) offers a therapeutically actionable solution to these
hurdles. Here, we will use biochemical engineering approaches to generate highly efficient RNA-targeting
CIRTS activators and degraders and prioritize those with optimized performance parameters using a
combination of disease-relevant target gene assays and in vivo immunogenicity studies.

title: Identifying the Genes that Function to Fuel RAS Driven SCCs
text:
Squamous cell carcinoma is a prevalent cancer arising in various epithelial tissues, often driven by mutations
in the RAS gene. Cancer stem cells within these tumors play a critical role in tumor progression and resistance
to therapy, largely through their interactions with the tumor microenvironment. This project aims to elucidate
the mechanism by which cancer stem cells in squamous cell carcinomas alter the tumor microenvironment to
drive squamous cell carcinoma progression.

title: Protein Intrinsic Disorder in Genome Regulation
text:
The integrity of our genome relies on the ability of cells to coordinate transcription, RNA processing, and DNA
repair. This research seeks to understand how flexible, disordered regions of proteins organize these essential
processes through the formation and regulation of nuclear condensates. By uncovering how biophysical
properties of condensates encode regulatory information, this work will provide new insights into the mechanisms
of genome maintenance and the molecular basis of human diseases such as neurodegeneration and cancer.

title: Signal transduction, cell biology and molecular pharmacology of ectopically expressed olfactory GPCR OR51E1
text:
Numerous chemical cues that regulate cell function in our bodies act via a family of proteins
known as G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs). The majority of known therapeutic drugs acts
on distinct members of this vast gene family. This project concentrates on OR51E1, an
understudied GPCR linked to prostate cancer and regulation of blood pressure. The proposed
experiments aim to elucidate the mechanism by which OR51E1 plays its role in these disorders
and discover novel small drug-like chemicals that can modulate activity of this receptor.

title: CHOLESTEROL METABOLISM IN THE PHARMACOLOGY OF LIPOSOMAL THERAPEUTICS
text:
This proposal will identify novel mechanisms by which liposomes are metabolized within the body and will
determine metabolites that alter immune function and tumor growth. The new knowledge generated is
expected to lead to the development of new cancer drug formulations that are both safer and more effective.
This proposal will also test new formulations of liposomal doxorubicin containing cholesterol analogs for the
treatment of cancer. Our results have the potential to have an immediate clinical impact by swiftly translating
into clinical trials. Since dysfunction in lipid metabolism is implicated in other health conditions, the application
of this knowledge extends beyond cancer therapy.

title: 3/4 Asian Bipolar Genetics Network (A-BIG-NET)
text: This proposal will leverage the Asian Bipolar Genetics Network (A-BIG-NET), an international collaboration of investigators from the U.S. and Asia, to carry out a molecular genetics study of bipolar disorder. It will establish a valuable genetics resource with 4x low-pass whole genome sequence and rich phenotype data that will dramatically increase the range of alleles that are studied from varying geographic origins in persons with bipolar disorder. This approach will accelerate gene discovery in this disorder and help U.S. citizens diagnosed with BP.

title: Neuroimaging and Electrophysiology Facility (NIEF)
text: The Neuroimaging and Electrophysiology Facility (NIEF) is a core with state-of-the-art instruments and experienced technical staff to support, guide and advice the scientific community in Puerto Rico. The main goal of this proposal is to maintain the NIEF services in microscopy or electrophysiological strategies and continue the positive impact of our investigators in terms of publications, grants submissions, grants funded, patents obtained and students who have completed their degrees by using the facilities. Excellent services and instruments in the NIEF at the Molecular Science Research Center and the Institute of Neurobiology, maximizes the impact of our cores to help investigators in the island and support the well-planned sustainability of the cores beyond COBRE-3.

title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Computer-Assisted Bilingual Vocabulary Intervention in Emergent Bilinguals with Developmental Language Disorder
text:
R&R Other Information
Project Narrative
Emergent Bilinguals with Developmental Language Disorder (DLD) often lack access to effective
bilingual intervention due to a shortage of bilingual professionals and the absence of intervention
approaches enabling monolingual English-speaking clinicians to support children’s first language
beyond passive encouragement. The proposed research is relevant to public health and NIDCD's
mission to improve the lives of individuals with communication disorders because it identifies if
computer-assisted bilingual vocabulary intervention (CABVI) approach for children with emergent
bilinguals with DLD is an effective intervention to support their bilingual vocabulary needs to
communicate successfully at home, school, and within their community. This project represents
a critical step towards using technologies to validate, recognize, and improve the bilingual
communication of emergent bilinguals with DLD.

title: Targeting MALT1 to Enhance Anti-Lymphoma Immunity and Response to Immunotherapy
text:
This project will pioneer an innovative approach to treat highly aggressive and therapy refractory B-cell
lymphomas (MCD-DLBCLs) using MALT1 targeted therapy, which interrupts key lymphomagenic pathways
and at the same time has the potential to disengage anti-lymphoma T-cell responses. Using newly developed
MCD-DLBCL models and fully immunocompetent syngeneic host mice in comparison with host mice lacking
specific arms of the immune system, we will elucidate the contribution of T-cell responses to the anti-
lymphoma activity of MALT1 inhibition. Building on this, we will establish optimal regimens of MALT1 inhibition
to enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy against MCD-DLBCLs in preclinical settings and study similar
effects of MALT1 inhibition in lymphoma patients enrolled in the first in human trial with a MALT1 inhibitor,
thus providing the proof-of-principle to investigate its combination with immunotherapy in the clinic.

title: An integrative study of gene-by-sleep and activity behavior interactions for cardiovascular health
text:
Prior gene–environment interaction (G×E) studies have shown that sleep duration and physical
activity can modify genetic risk factors for cardiovascular health (CVH) outcomes, but findings
remain limited. Building on the collaborative efforts of the established Gene–Lifestyle Interaction
Working Group within the Cohorts for Heart and Aging Research in Genomic Epidemiology
(CHARGE) consortium, we will conduct multi-level G×E analyses of CVH outcomes across
multiple cohorts and biobanks, leveraging objective exposure measures, rare variants, and
longitudinal data. This study will provide new insights into how sleep and activity behaviors
interact with molecular pathways underlying CVH, ultimately informing future strategies for
cardiovascular disease prevention and intervention.

title: The Role of SECTM1 in Monocyte Biology and Atherosclerosis
text:
Despite significant advances in preventative therapies for coronary heart disease, there is a significant residual
burden of disease, in part due to the role of vascular inflammation in the development of atherosclerosis. The
goal of this proposal is to delineate new pathways contributing to the inflammatory risk in atherosclerosis using
an integrative omics approach, combining emerging proteomic profiling techniques, human genetics,
bioinformatics and small animal models of disease.

title: RESP-FIT: A Respiratory Muscle Strength Training Intervention for COPD
text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a leading cause of death and decreased quality of life, particularly among individuals living in rural areas. This project will test a home-based, technology-supported respiratory muscle training program designed to reduce shortness of breath and improve daily functioning and quality of life in adults with COPD. Findings from this research will support development of scalable approaches to improve respiratory health for individuals with COPD living in rural communities.

title: Immunologic and Imaging studies with TNF Therapy in Prodromal Synucleinopathies
text:
PRISMS is a prospective, randomized clinical trial testing the ability of the anti-TNFα (adalimumab) to slow or
prevent the progression of motor and cognitive symptoms of synucleinopathy in persons with REM Sleep
Behavior Disorder with core funding provided by the Marcus Foundation. The design of the study provides the
substrate for longitudinal assessments to explore not only the effect of the therapeutic intervention, by performing
1) in vivo perturb seq to identify changes in immune cell function after anti-TNFα treatment in CSF and blood
using single cell RNA sequencing; 2) characterization immune cell populations, with a focus on FoxP3 regulatory
CD4 T cells; 3) evaluation of the soluble markers of inflammation and neurodegeneration in blood and CSF; 4)
multimodal imaging studies, including brain metabolic patterns assessed using 18-F Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)
and integrity of dopamine and catecholamine neurons using Dopamine Transporter (DaT) SPECT and
neuromelanin MRI imaging and 5) assessment of motor and cognitive function using sensitive digital health
technologies in addition to routine clinical scales. In this proposal, we are requesting funding to support for
conducting novel mechanistic studies While the clinical trial will test the hypothesis that prodromal PD as manifest
with RBD is inflammatory mediated by TNFα, whether or not the treatment approach is successful, this project
will provide deep mechanistic insight into the role of the TNF pathway in the progression of synucleinopathies.
